Neonates of the gray whale (Eschrichtius robustus) emerge from the birth canal after a gestation period of 395 days [tg = 395 days] at a core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a duration that reflects the considerable energy investment required to produce a large, precocial calf. At the moment of parturition, a newborn calf typically measures 450 centimeters [Lb = 450 centimeters] in total length and carries a wet weight of 500,000 grams [Wwb = 500,000 grams]. This substantial birth mass, equivalent to half a metric ton, is characteristic of baleen whales and allows the neonate to withstand the thermal challenges of the cold marine environment. The suckling calf depends entirely on its mother’s lipid-rich milk, which supports rapid somatic growth during the initial months of life. Field observations indicate that the period of nutritional dependence, from birth until the cessation of lactation, spans approximately 180 days [tx = approximately 180 days] at 38 °C [T = 38 °C], after which the weaned juvenile begins to forage independently on benthic invertebrates.

As the young whale matures, it undergoes a prolonged developmental trajectory before reaching reproductive competence. The transition from a dependent calf to a self-sufficient juvenile is marked by the acquisition of foraging skills necessary to exploit dense patches of ampeliscid amphipods in the soft sediments of the Bering and Chukchi seas. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis, is attained at 2,922 days after birth (2922 days after birth) [tp = 2922 days after birth] under the thermal conditions of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a remarkably late maturation event even among large cetaceans. This delayed onset of reproductive activity is likely linked to the extensive period required for skeletal and energetic development. During the sub-adult phase, individuals continue to increase in body size, gradually approaching the dimensions characteristic of fully grown adults. The protracted juvenile period also allows calves to learn complex migratory routes that span thousands of kilometers between high-latitude feeding grounds and warm-water breeding lagoons along the Baja California peninsula.

Adult gray whales achieve an ultimate total length of 1,520 centimeters (1520 cm) [Li = 1520 cm], making them one of the larger members of the family Eschrichtiidae, though they remain smaller than many of their balaenopterid relatives. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a reproductively mature individual reaches 28,500,000 grams [Wwi = 28,500,000 grams], a massive body size that necessitates prodigious daily food intake during the summer feeding season. This enormous biomass is sustained by a filter-feeding strategy in which the whale rolls onto its side and engulfs sediment-laden water, straining out crustaceans through its coarse baleen plates. The species exhibits marked sexual dimorphism, with females typically attaining slightly larger body dimensions than males, a pattern that may relate to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. Comparative analyses with other mysticetes suggest that the relatively modest adult length of the gray whale, compared to the blue whale, reflects evolutionary trade-offs between body size and the costs of migration.

Reproductive output in the gray whale is best characterized through the components of fecundity and breeding frequency. Females typically produce a single calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = single calf per reproductive event], a litter size that is invariant across most baleen whale species and reflects the substantial maternal investment required for each offspring. The interval between successive births is approximately one calf every two years [F_R_i = approximately one calf every two years], with a biennial cycle that allows the female to recover her body condition after the prolonged period of lactation. These combined parameters yield a maximum reproductive rate that is moderate compared to smaller mammalian species, highlighting the life-history strategy of producing few, well-provisioned offspring in an unpredictable pelagic environment. The observed twinning rate is exceptionally low, and instances of successfully rearing both calves are virtually unknown in wild populations.

Longevity data for the gray whale, derived from analyses of earplug laminae and photo-identification studies of known individuals, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 28,105 days [am = approximately 28,105 days] at 38 °C [T = 38 °C], which corresponds to roughly 77 years. This remarkable longevity places the species among the longest-lived cetaceans, surpassed only by the bowhead whale, which can exceed two centuries. The extended lifespan is consistent with a slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturity, low annual fecundity, and high maternal investment per offspring. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with older individuals showing reduced foraging efficiency and increased scar tissue from predation attempts by killer whales. The ecological significance of such longevity includes the accumulation of traditional knowledge about migratory routes and feeding sites, which may be transmitted across generations through social learning within matrilineal groups.
